Molecular epidemiology of Dobrava-Belgrade virus in Greece
Katerina Tsergouli, Elpida Papadopoulou, Katerina Tsioka, Anna Papa⁎
Department of Microbiology, Medical School, Aristotle University of Thessaloniki, Thessaloniki, Greece
A R T I C L E I N F O
Keywords:
Hantavirus
Dobrava-Belgrade virus
Greece
A B S T R A C T
In order to gain an insight into the genetic relatedness of the Dobrava-Belgrade virus (DOBV) in Greece, a
phylogenetic analysis was performed based on all currently available DOBV sequences obtained from hospita-
lized cases with hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS). Most cases occurred in northwestern and north
central part of the country. Two sequence datasets consisted of 41 S and 12 M partial DOBV RNA segment
sequences were analyzed. All DOBV strains belong to Dobrava genotype which is associated with the rodent
Apodemus flavicollis. In both phylogenetic trees (S and M segments), two main clusters of Greek strains could be
distinguished. Phylogenetic analysis showed a spatial rather than temporal relation of the strains, since their
genetic clustering was highly associated with the geographic distribution of the cases. Besides previous char-
acterized endemic foci, novel ones have been identified, expanding our knowledge on the epidemiology of HFRS
in Greece.
1. Introduction
Hantaviruses (genus Orthohantavirus, family Hantaviridae) are
single-stranded, negative-sense RNA viruses with a three-segmented
genome consisting of the S (small), M (medium) and L (large) segments
which encode the nucleocapsid protein (N), a precursor protein giving
rise to the two envelope glycoproteins Gn and Gc, and the RNA-de-
pendent RNA polymerase (RdRp), respectively (Battisti et al., 2011;
Schmaljohn et al., 1985). Hantaviruses are transmitted to humans
through inhalation of infected rodents' excreta. While hantaviruses
cause to rodents a persistent and asymptomatic infection, they cause to
humans two severe syndromes: hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome
(HFRS) in Europe and Asia, and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome in the
Americas. More than 40 hantavirus species have been currently re-
cognized, each of them associated with a specific rodent host, while
spill-over events have been also described (Jonsson et al., 2010).
The main hantaviruses in Europe are Dobrava-Belgrade virus
(DOBV) associated with rodents of the Apodemus species, and Puumala
virus (PUUV) associated with Myodes glareolus rodents. A sub-division
of DOBV species into 4 genotypes, Dobrava, Kurkino, Saaremaa, and
Sochi, has been proposed; the primary rodent hosts of Dobrava and
Sochi genotypes are Apodemus flavicollis and Apodemus ponticus rodents,
respectively, whereas Apodemus agrarius serves as host of Saaremaa and
Kurkino genotypes (Klempa et al., 2012). The most severe form of HFRS
is caused by Dobrava and Sochi genotypes. The disease is characterized
by fever, myalgia, thrombocytopenia, and acute renal insufficiency; the
case fatality rate is
9 \mathrm { - } 1 5 \%
(Papa, 2012; Kruger et al., 2015).
Greece is located in the southernmost region of the Balkan peninsula
in the southwestern Europe. Since the first serological evidence of
hantavirus presence in Greece in 1981 (Lee and Antoniadis, 1981), the
annual reported number of HFRS cases is 2–10, with approximate
fatality
(Papa et al., 1998; Papa, 2012). It is believed that some mild
cases remain unrecognized. Since the first direct genetic detection of
DOBV in two HFRS patients in 1996 in Greece (Antoniadis et al., 1996),
molecular methods were included for the laboratory diagnosis of han-
tavirus infections in the country. A retrospective study showed that all
PCR-positive hospitalized cases in Greece were caused by DOBV asso-
ciated with A. flavicollis (Dobrava genotype) (Papa et al., 1998). The
number of PUUV cases is limited [(Papa et al., 2000) and few un-
published cases].
As more sequences from Greek HFRS cases became available during
the last 20 years, the aim of the present study was to gain an overall
insight into the molecular epidemiology of DOBV in Greece by in-
vestigating the spatial and temporal genetic relationships among viral
strains detected in the country.
2. Materials and methods
The study was based on all DOBV sequences currently available
from Greece. They were obtained from 27 HFRS cases observed during
the last 20 years in Greece by applying two nested RT-PCRs: one am-
plifying a 599-bp fragment of the S RNA segment and a second am-
plifying a 317-bp fragment of the M RNA segment from hantaviruses
associated with rodents of the Muridae subfamily (Papa et al., 1998).

4. Discussion
Greece is situated on the crossroads of Europe, Asia and Africa,
located at the southernmost tip of the Balkan peninsula. The first direct
genetic detection of DOBV in two HFRS patients was reported in 1996
in Greece, providing evidence that DOBV can cause severe disease in
humans (Antoniadis et al., 1996). Besides Greece, DOBV has been often
detected in HFRS patients and in rodent virus reservoirs in several
Balkan countries (Emmerich et al., 2014; Papa and Christova, 2006,
2011, 2016; Stamenkovic et al., 2015; Avsic-Zupanc et al., 1999).
Furthermore, DOBV sequences have been detected in A. flavicollis ro-
dents trapped in the European part of Turkey and in the Black Sea re-
gion (Polat et al., 2018; Oktem et al., 2014).
The areas where Dobrava genotype infections are observed coincide
with the typical habitats of A. flavicollis, the yellow necked mouse,
which is the main reservoir of the virus. This rodent species prefers the
non-inhabited forested or shrubby areas with altitude ranging from 150
to
1 3 5 0 \mathrm { m }
above sea level (Rogozi et al., 2012). Based on an earlier
study which was based on HFRS cases observed in Greece up to 1996,
the most endemic foci were in the northwestern and northeastern parts
of the country, where Pindus and Rodopi mountains predominate, re-
spectively (Papa et al., 1998). Pindus is a range of high altitude
mountains and it is considered a continuation of the Dinaric Alps
crossing vertically Greece and separating naturally the western and
eastern mainland of Greece. Rodopi mountain ranges horizontally in
the northeastern part of Greece and forms a natural boundary with
Bulgaria. Since 1996, additional cases were observed in the known
endemic foci, but also in novel areas where no cases have been reported
previously, expanding the geographic distribution of the virus to
southern regions. Among overall cases, most occurred in Epirus
, and in central and western Macedonia
and
respectively). A strong relation between genetic clustering and geo-
graphic location was seen, reflecting the limited range of rodents' ac-
tivity.
Phylogenetic analysis showed that the Greek DOBV strains belong to
the Dobrava genotype and cluster together with respective strains from
other Balkan countries, with which they share a common ancestry.
Specifically, clade A consisting of Dobrava sequences from the north-
eastern part of the country, clusters together with Albanian strains,
while clade B, consisting from Dobrava sequences from the north-
western part of the country, clusters together with Bulgarian strains
(Fig. 1). Several mountains separate geographically the mainland of
Greece, and form local ecosystems in which Dobrava virus evolved
through the years, giving rise to subgroups in the phylogeny. It is of
interest that the sequences from two cases observed in the same pre-
fecture (cases 167/05 and 73/02 observed in Magnesia prefecture)
clustered into different clades, A and B, respectively, suggesting that
either this region might represent the meeting zone of the two clades, or
the location where any of the two patients was infected was different
than that reported.
In conclusion, the present study provides further insight into the
molecular epidemiology of DOBV in Greece and gives evidence that at
present the PCR-positive cases are caused by Dobrava genotype, which
shows a strong geographic distribution. Awareness among clinicians is
needed to include HFRS in the differential diagnosis of febrile cases
with thrombocytopenia and acute renal insufficiency in order to elu-
cidate further the epidemiology of HFRS in Greece and study in more
detail the virus spread and evolution.
